title: Reason, Then Re-reason: Cross-view Revisiting Improves Spatial Reasoning
claim: Single-turn inference makes spatial errors from limited views; revisiting with a complementary synthesized view lets the model correct its answer.
layout: 2 stacked cases, video frame strips left, reasoning text boxes right, red circles
description: The figure has two stacked cases, (a) object counting and (b) route planning. In each case, a strip of eight egocentric video frames labeled 'Original-view' sits above a strip of eight synthesized 'Novel-view' frames, which are elevated and oblique. Red dashed circles on the novel-view frames mark the evidence that was missed, such as an occluded chair or a bookshelf. A question appears under each strip. Next to each question, a ground-truth label sits beside a blue 'Baseline' answer and a red 'ReRe' answer. On the right, dashed boxes hold the chain-of-thought text. Blue text marks the Reason Phase output and red text marks the Re-Reason Phase output, which corrects the earlier answer. The eye goes first to the photo strips and the red circles.
caption: ReRe enables the model to revisit its initial hypothesis under a synthesized novel view, correcting spatial reasoning errors that single-turn inference misses. Each case shows the original egocentric video (top frames) and the synthesized novel view (bottom frames), along with the model’s reasoning before (Reason Phase, blue) and after (Re-Reason Phase, red) revisiting. (a) Object Counting: The synthesized elevated view reveals a chair occluded by the desk, prompting the model to correct its initial count. (b) Route Planning: The expanded perspective exposes a previously unobserved target, enabling the model to revise its hallucinated command.
abstract: Spatial reasoning from egocentric videos is inherently challenging because the observable evidence is constrained by the camera trajectory. Existing methods rely on single-turn inference, forcing models to resolve geometric ambiguity through semantic priors rather than verifiable evidence. We argue that spatial reasoning should be revisitable: conclusions formed under limited evidence should remain open to revision when complementary viewpoints become available. Building on this insight, we propose Reason, then Re-reason (ReRe), a training-free, inference-time framework with two phases: in the Reason Phase, an MLLM forms a spatial hypothesis from the original video; in the Re-reason Phase, it verifies or revises the hypothesis by observing a synthesized novel-view video. To enable effective cross-view revisiting, we design a Geometry-to-Video pipeline that renders strategically complementary novel views from predicted 3D geometry. These views feature an elevated, oblique perspective with scene-spanning coverage, while preserving the MLLM's native video interface without architectural modifications. Extensive evaluations on VSI-Bench and STI-Bench demonstrate that ReRe substantially boosts open-source MLLMs to rival proprietary state-of-the-art performance. Project page: https://zhenjiemao.github.io/ReRe/
